engine.heading: Where the numbers come from
engine.body:
Every forecast is worked out on this device by the core physics behind VOACAP, a propagation model that has been in use for decades. The core physics are the same whichever model you pick.

This app offers two models:

1. VOACAP, which was written by the US government's Institute for Telecommunication Sciences. It is reproduced faithfully here, including a small number of defects that were in the original model. This model uses a monthly average. While each time of day is different, each day in the same month is not. So 4pm this Tuesday looks the same as 4pm this Thursday.

2. Truecast, which works from what the ionosphere is actually doing that day. Scored day by day against real measurements since 2015, it was closer than VOACAP on 77% of days, and its average miss was about a fifth smaller. More on Truecast below.

truecast.heading: Truecast, the newer model
truecast.body:
Truecast is this app's own model based on VOACAP physics but adjusts for what the ionosphere is doing on the day instead of for a typical day of the month.

Along with daily granularity, a daily sunspot figure worked out from ionosonde stations, a table of magnetic storms, and a better calculation of the height a signal bounces from all change how this forecast is calculated.

This model was built and checked against ionosonde readings covering a full solar cycle, from 2015 to today. It was then scored on eight months it had never seen, chosen in advance to span quiet and stormy conditions. On those months it removed the month-to-month bias VOACAP carries, and it was closer to the measured values in seven of those eight months.

Like the VOACAP model, it needs no network. With no connection it uses a built-in correction for the time of year, and is still better than the monthly average.

You can switch to VOACAP at any time in Preferences. Changing the model recomputes the forecast and the map.

ssn.heading: The sunspot number
ssn.body:
The smoothed sunspot number for the month is the largest driver of the prediction model. The bands, the hours and the paths all follow from it.

Figures for every month from {{first}} to {{last}} are built into the app, so a forecast needs no network. Months ahead use the published prediction, which can be revised later.

When a reading of solar and magnetic conditions is less than {{hours}} hours old, the app uses that instead. After that it goes back to the monthly figure.

colours.heading: What the colors mean
colours.body: A color is the chance of making the contact, not how strong the signal will be. Reliable means about {{reliable}} times in 100 or better, patchy at least {{patchy}} in 100, and weak at least {{weak}} in 100. Below that the band is considered closed.

map.heading: How the map is drawn
map.body:
A rough map of the world is drawn first, so there is something to read at once with a finer map of {{points}} places showing up as its calculations are completed.

A map does not change within a month and so the app keeps the maps it has already computed, and can make them before you need them — see Compute maps ahead in this menu.

invertedV.heading: A note on the inverted V
invertedV.body:
VOACAP has no inverted V internally. Instead the app calculates an inverted V as a dipole at {{percent}}% of the apex height. If the apex is 10 meters, the model uses 8 meters.

For a horizontal wire, the height above ground sets the gain straight up. An inverted V has its ends lower than its apex, so it behaves like a dipole below the apex. Near vertical, a horizontal wire radiates almost the same in all directions, so which way the wire runs changes little.

This is an approximation, not a measurement. A V with steep legs behaves lower than this, and a shallow V behaves higher. Select the dipole if your wire is level.

nvis.heading: Near-vertical incidence
nvis.body:
Below a few hundred kilometers, the low bands work in a different way. The signal goes up steeply, comes back down near where it started, and there is no skip zone. Operators call this NVIS.

The app does not guess this from the distance. The engine calculates the angle the signal leaves at, and the app calls a path near-vertical when that angle is {{degrees}} degrees or more and the band works.

The map puts dots on the area that reaches you this way. The dots are separate from the colors, because the colors already show the chance of contact. The line below the map gives the distance in words.
